implementation_notes: Kotlin multiplatform projects use kotlinx.atomicfu, which provides atomic types as inline classes over the platform's primitives - AtomicInt, AtomicLong, AtomicRef - with zero allocation on the JVM (the value is inlined into the field) and real atomics on Native and JS. That is why atomicfu exists rather than relying on java.util.concurrent.atomic: a value class avoids boxing and is the only form that works on Kotlin/Native. Plain Kotlin on the JVM can of course use java.util.concurrent.atomic directly, and coroutines' Mutex is usually the better answer when you do not need lock-freedom.
idiom_name: kotlinx.atomicfu AtomicInt/AtomicLong/AtomicRef (inline classes) or java.util.concurrent.atomic on the JVM
pitfalls: atomicfu's atomic are inline classes, so an AtomicInt parameter is unboxed at the call boundary and cannot be stored in a generic collection without boxing.
On Kotlin/Native the old memory model (before 1.7.20) froze threads at object field access; verify the runtime version before assuming field-level concurrency works at all.
kotlinx.atomicfu transforms bytecode (a compiler plugin), which must be applied in every module or the code silently uses the fallback - a build configuration trap, not a code one.
Coroutines' Mutex is often the right answer: an atomic spin loop inside a coroutine on a single-threaded dispatcher never makes progress.
alternative: kotlinx.coroutines Mutex for mutual exclusion, or an actor/scope-confined state for cooperative concurrency
